title: Wavefront
content: A wavefront is defined as a surface associated with a propagating wave which is a locus of all points having the same phase if the wave.
e: A wavefront is the surface through all points of a travelling wave that share the same phase. Rays are perpendicular to that surface. Far from a point source the spherical wavefront flattens into a plane wavefront.

title: Phase (Phase Angle)
content: The angular position of a point of a periodic wave is known as the phase angle.
e: Phase angle is the angular position of a point of a periodic wave on a reference circle at a given instant. It is not a length along a straight line. One full cycle runs from 0 to 2 pi.

title: Phase Difference
content: The difference states of the periodic waves at the same instant is represented by phase difference. The phase difference is the difference in the phase angle of two waves.
e: Phase difference compares the phase angles of two waves at the same instant. A difference of 0 or 2 pi means they swing together. A difference of pi means they swing opposite, fully out of phase.

title: Path Difference
content: Path difference indicates the distance between two points measured along the direction of propagation of the wave through the medium.
e: Path difference is the extra distance one wave travels, measured along the propagation direction. It is not a sideways gap. Path difference of m lambda puts the waves in phase; odd half-wavelengths put them out of phase.

title: Interference of Light
content: Wave interference is the phenomenon that occurs when two waves meet while traveling along the same medium. If light waves interference with one another, the maximum and the minimum intensity of light are obtained alternatively.
e: Interference happens when two waves meet in the same medium. Superposition makes bright maxima and dark minima in turn. Coherent sources of the same frequency and a steady phase difference are what make a stable pattern.

title: Interference of light waves
content: Interference of light waves is defined as the modification in the distribution of light energy (intensity) when two or more waves superimposes each other.
e: Interference of light waves is the change in how light energy is spread when two or more waves superpose. Intensity is no longer uniform. Bright and dark fringes appear instead of a flat wash of light.

title: Fringe width
content: Distance between two adjacent bright (or dark) fringes is called the fringe width.
e: Fringe width is the distance between two neighbouring bright fringes, or two neighbouring dark fringes. It equals lambda D over d in Young's arrangement. Alternate fringes, skipping one, are not how you define that spacing.

title: Diffraction of light
content: Diffraction is defined as the bending of waves around the corners of an obstacle (or) through an aperture into the region of geometrical shadow of the obstacle (or) aperture.
e: Diffraction is the bending of waves around an obstacle or through an aperture into the geometrical shadow. The bending is obvious when the opening is comparable to the wavelength. Reflection off a mirror is a different process.

title: Fresnel Diffraction
content: The source of light and the screen are at a finite distance from the obstacle causing the diffraction.
e: In Fresnel diffraction the source and the screen sit at finite distances from the obstacle, so the wavefront is still curved. You cannot treat the incoming wave as plane. Fraunhofer diffraction is the infinite-distance limit.

title: Fraunhofer diffraction
content: There is an infinite distance between the source and the screen from the obstacle.
e: In Fraunhofer diffraction the source and the screen are effectively infinitely far from the obstacle, so the wavefront is plane. Lenses are often used to reach that limit in the lab. Fresnel work keeps finite distances.

title: Diffraction Grating
content: A diffraction grating is a component of optical devices which consists of a large number of parallel slits of same width separated by equal opaque spaces.
e: A diffraction grating is many parallel slits of equal width, separated by equal opaque spaces. It spreads light into wavelength components for spectroscopy. Transmission and reflection are the two main types, not absorption gratings.

title: The grating constant (N)
content: The number of lines (or) slits per unit length (lines per cm) is called the grating constant.
e: The grating constant N is the number of lines or slits per unit length, not per unit area. The slit spacing d is 1/N. A larger N packs the slits closer and fans the colours out more.
